transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Dana (NeuroScale ML), Rajiv (Infra), Sofia (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be partial):
- Detailed runtime discussion focused on Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen behavior under batching and KV cache workloads; MoE routing overhead and rope (RoPE) positional scaling impacts were main topics.
- Action items: benchmarks to run, prompt sets to be shared, and plan for on-prem pilot.

Topics: 
- Model-specific kernel selection and quantization tradeoffs
- MoE routing costs and memory/throughput implications
- RoPE scaling issues when extending context beyond pretraining dims
- KV cache warm/cold paths and prefix caching strategies
- Batching heuristics vs latency SLOs and autoscale knobs
- VPC/on-prem considerations and audit/logging
Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, excited to dig into the performance questions you had. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Dana: Dana here. Hi.
[00:07] Rajiv: Rajiv on infra.
[00:09] Sofia: Sofia.
[00:11] Marco: Marco from Redwood SE.
[00:13] Aisha: Great. Quick agenda — Marco will walk through measurements we've done and some model-specific notes (Llama, Mistral, Qwen), then we can go into your workloads and plan benchmarks.
[00:20] Marco: Cool, jumping in. So we split this into five buckets: kernel choice and attention implementation, KV cache behavior, batching/throughput, quantization/bitwidths, and MoE/rope special cases. I'll start with a high-level that you can interrupt.
[01:02] Dana: Please — interrupt a lot. We have a few weird behaviors when we push context to 64k tokens, especially with Llama-variants — latencies spike non-linearly.
[01:12] Marco: Right, expected. Two things: first, RoPE scaling — many open checkpoints assume base RoPE frequencies up to pretraining max length; when you push to 64k, you hit interpolation/extrapolation modes and that changes numerical stability and the attention kernel's memory working set. Second, KV cache indexing grows linearly so cache walking and scatter/gather overhead show up in both memory and kernel launch overheads.
[01:53] Rajiv: Can you unpack the RoPE thing? We saw weird repetition and odd token placement after 32k. Is that the same?
[02:05] Marco: Yeah, when you extrapolate RoPE beyond the positional frequencies it was tuned for, you sometimes see phase aliasing. Practically, that looks like repetition or positional drift. On the runtime side there are two levers: one is pre-scaling hooks where we remap position encodings using a linear rescale factor (we've got a doc link) — this adds a tiny compute but keeps numerical stability. The other is attention kernel tiling — if you change tile sizes to favor longer sequences you reduce kernel launch count but increase per-kernel memory, tradeoff between latency and TDP.
[02:55] Dana: That remap — is it compatible with Llama and Mistral variants? Qwen?
[03:02] Marco: Generally yes but with caveats. Llama-2 family uses rotary embeddings similar to classic RoPE; Mistral has slightly different rotary parameterization (they use different freq schedule sometimes), and Qwen has some proprietary tweaks — we treat Qwen as a case-by-case. Our runtime exposes a "rope-scaling" flag per model that applies the remap and a fallback to chunked attention for very long contexts.
[03:35] Rajiv: Chunked attention — that means degrading quality?
[03:40] Marco: Slightly. Chunked/strided attention can reduce cross-chunk interactions; we document that as a quality tradeoff. For many retrieval-augmented tasks it doesn't hurt output quality much; for pure generative long-form, results vary.
[03:55] Sofia: Can you explain MoE routing cost? We're evaluating an MoE architecture for some multi-domain tasks.
[04:02] Marco: Sure. MoE introduces conditional compute — only a subset of experts run per token. That sounds cheaper but routing has its own costs: gather/scatter around experts, cross-device communication if experts are sharded, and padding/slot-filling for batch alignment. Two common runtime effects: tail latency spikes on imbalanced inputs and throughput drop when batch sizes are small because dispatch overhead dominates.
[04:45] Dana: So if we run MoE on dedicated GPUs, does Redwood help with expert placement?
[04:50] Marco: Yes — in Dedicated and Private we can pin experts to devices and optimize routing to minimize cross-device comms. We also have a routing-aware batcher that tries to group tokens by expert to amortize the scatter/gather. That helps but requires consistent workload distribution; for highly skewed traffic you'll still see imbalances.
[05:20] Rajiv: What's the impact on KV cache size with MoE?
[05:25] Marco: Slightly higher metadata overhead: the KV cache still stores key/value per active attention head, but MoE's different experts may have different head dims, and routing metadata needs a per-token expert id which we store alongside the cache entry. So memory grows modestly and gains complexity for eviction/serialization in on-prem snapshots.
[05:55] Aisha: Quick pause — we had a question about quantization, Mistral specifically.
[06:01] Dana: Yes, Mistral-7B quantized to 4-bit looks great cost-wise but we see more hallucination in some prompts.
[06:08] Marco: Known tradeoff — aggressive quantization (4-bit) can introduce small operator-level bias, especially in LayerNorm and softmax paths. Our recommendation: for sensitive QA or when you need faithful arithmetic, keep LayerNorm & final projection in fp16 and quantize weights elsewhere (a hybrid scheme). For Mistral we've validated a q4_hybrid that keeps norms in fp16 and reduces hallucination relative to blind q4.
[06:40] Dana: Does Redwood runtime handle mixed-precision per-op?
[06:44] Marco: Yes, our kernel selection supports per-op precision hooks; we generate execution plans that mix fp16 and int4 paths. This costs slightly more memory and scheduling complexity but usually retains much of the speed gain.
[06:55] Rajiv: On the batching front — we saw Redwood's docs about continuous batching. Can you explain how that affects our latency SLOs?
[07:03] Marco: Continuous batching accumulates tokens until a batch cost threshold or latency SLO triggers a flush. With small SLOs (say <50ms) the system favors low-latency mode and you get tiny batches; with relaxed SLOs you get more batching and better throughput. There are tuning knobs: max_batch_tokens, max_batch_size, and adaptive_delay. For MoE we add an expert-aware delay that tries to accumulate same-expert tokens.
[07:40] Dana: Any numbers you can share from your internal runs?
[07:45] Marco: Quick snapshot: Llama-2-70B fp16 single request 16-token completion on an A100 — median p95 latency ~320ms cold, ~180ms warm with KV cache. Mistral-7B quant q4_hybrid single request 16-token median p95 ~95ms warm. Qwen-14B numbers vary; on some kernels Qwen optimizations make it close to Llama-3 at same size. But these are workload dependent.
[08:25] Sofia: The p95 difference is big. How much does KV cache help for long contexts?
[08:29] Marco: If you have repeated prefixes or retrieval-augmented flows, KV cache warm paths reduce the incremental token cost — some of our tests show 2.5-3x token throughput on warm vs cold for long prefix lengths, but warm speed depends on cache memory layout and scatter/gather cost. Warm also depends on whether prefix is shared across requests (we can shard cache by session to reduce duplication).
[09:00] Rajiv: For on-prem, what's the recommended eviction strategy if we have limited GPU memory?
[09:07] Marco: We recommend a tiered cache: active sessions in GPU, less-active in host DRAM, and cold snapshots to NFS. Eviction is LRU or frequency-based; for very long contexts we implement a ring buffer per session so you can keep a sliding window without linear growth.
[09:30] Dana: Anything else on networking? We're concerned about cross-node bandwidth for MoE.
[09:35] Marco: Absolutely — MoE benefits from RDMA-level bandwidth for cross-device expert calls. On-prem we recommend 100GbE+ RDMA fabric and pinning experts within a rack. In Dedicated we deploy expert pools co-located to reduce inter-az hops.
[09:58] Aisha: Quick question for the team: any gotchas with model sharding + quantization?
[10:04] Marco: Two gotchas: 1) int4 kernels currently have less mature CUDA kernels for scattered matmuls, so you may see lower efficiency on sharded models if the communication/compression ratio is high. 2) Calibration: per-shard quant scales need consistent calibration — mismatch causes accuracy drift. We include a shard-consistent quantizer in our Optimize toolkit.
[10:35] Dana: On rope scaling again — is the remap deterministic and reversible? We need deterministic outputs for audit.
[10:41] Marco: The remap is deterministic given the same seed and parameters. The transformation isn't reversible in a lossless sense (it's a linear rescale), but it doesn't inject nondeterminism. For strict audit you can pin the rope-scaling flag and include it in inference metadata.
[11:05] Rajiv: How about logging and audit in Private/VPC? We need to capture per-token timings and routing logs for compliance.
[11:12] Marco: Private supports verbose tracing with minimal overhead — we stream routing metadata, token timings, and kernel selection to a local collector; storing is optional. For regulated customers we can redact token text and persist metadata only.
[11:30] Sofia: Suppose we do a pilot — what would Redwood need from us to make the bench accurate?
[11:35] Marco: Three things: (1) prompt distributions and representative sessions (2) target SLOs and cost targets so we can tune batching and quantization heuristics, (3) hardware profile — are you testing on A100, H100, or Ampere/Blackwell equivalents?
[11:50] Dana: We'll provide the traces and SLOs.
[11:52] Marco: Great. We'll run: warm/cold KV runs, MoE skew experiments, rope extrapolation tests at 16k/32k/64k, and quantization fidelity runs. We'll put results in a shared spreadsheet and annotate kernels.
[12:10] Aisha: Quick wrap — recap next steps and owners?
[12:15] Marco: I'll run the bench and upload — see action item.
[12:17] Dana: I'll send prompts and the histograms.
[12:19] Aisha: I'll share pricing and the rope/quant docs.
[12:22] Sofia: Sounds good — thanks.
[12:25] Aisha: End of meeting.

Notes on transcription: There's usual small transcription errors — "KV cash" for KV cache in one spot, timings are approximate.
